entry.title: The puzzle in your browser
entry.summary: Today’s puzzle now plays on the website: the same puzzle as the app, a fourth copy of the rules, and what the page leaves out on purpose.
entry.content:
A game with a new mechanic has a problem a screenshot cannot solve. Nobody knows what “the pearls drift” means until they have made one drift. From today the day’s puzzle plays in a browser, on a phone or at a desk, with nothing to install and no account.

The same puzzle as the app

The app sets one puzzle a day: a position, a side to move, and one to four moves in which to force a pearl onto your shore whatever the other side answers. The book holds eighty of them, and the app walks through it in a fixed order that mixes the short puzzles with the long ones. The page takes the same walk. So the page and the app show the same puzzle on the same day, and in both the day turns over at midnight where you are.

A wrong move is played out

In the app, a move that does not solve the puzzle is refused. The board jolts, a line of text says why, and nothing moves. That suits a player who already knows the game.

Someone meeting the page may never have seen a pearl drift. So the page plays the wrong move: the anchor lands, the pearls slide, the page says it was not the one, and the board goes back. The hope is that a few wrong moves show the rules better than a paragraph can. The paragraphs are in Why the pearls drift. The tries are counted, and the count goes into the result you can share.

A fourth copy of the rules

The rules already existed three times: in Python, in Rust, and in Swift for the app. A browser runs none of those, so they were written once more, in JavaScript.

A fourth copy is a fourth chance to be wrong, and a puzzle page that drifted a pearl the wrong way would teach a game that does not exist. So before the page went up, every legal move from every position on every solution in the book was played twice, once by the JavaScript rules and once by the Python ones, and the boards were compared. That came to 15,233 moves and no differences.

Then the check was tested the way a smoke alarm is. Six faults were planted in the rules, one at a time. It caught five. The sixth removed the rule that a pearl may not drift onto a square where another pearl stood, and nothing changed, for a good reason: a pearl is never pulled toward the pearl beside it, because that pearl blocks the pull. The line guards against something the other rules already rule out.

What the page leaves out

One puzzle a day, and only today’s. No hints, no streak, no archive. Those are in the app, along with everything a puzzle is not: an opponent who fights back, a friend across the table, the daily game and its leaderboard.

On an iPhone or iPad the page plays three daily puzzles and then points to the app, where the daily puzzle is free. A phone that can run the game should run the game. Anywhere else, the page never stops you.

The page remembers the days you solved in your own browser, so it can say so when you come back, and it sends nothing anywhere. The privacy policy has the details.

entry.title: Why the pearls drift
entry.summary: The one rule the whole game hangs on, and the four small rules that keep it from stalling.
entry.content:
Most board games move pieces. In Swan Road you never move a pearl. You place an anchor, and the pearls move themselves.

The pull

An anchor pulls a pearl when they share a row or column, are at most three squares apart, and nothing stands between them. Touching pulls with 3, two squares away with 2, three away with 1. Every anchor pulls toward itself, whoever owns it.

That last part matters more than it sounds. Your opponent’s anchors pull too, so a pearl near their anchor is in their hands even when it sits in front of yours. The board is never “my side” and “your side”. It is one stretch of water, and every anchor on it is tugging.

The drift

After every turn, each pearl adds up the pulls on it: up minus down, right minus left. It moves one square along whichever total is larger. If the totals are equal, or there are none, it stays. All the moving pearls move at once.

Equal pulls cancel. That line is the heart of the game. An anchor is not only a way to bring a pearl toward you; it is a way to hold a pearl still against someone else’s anchor. Two anchors facing each other across a pearl make a standoff, and the next anchor either side places decides it.

A pearl arrives on a shore row and is collected by whoever owns that shore. First to three wins.

Four small rules

Those two rules make a game, but on their own they make a slow one. Thousands of games between two copies of the computer player, played in a simulator before the app existed, found the places it stalled. Four rules fix them.

  1. The first four turns are setup. Nothing drifts until turn five. Without that, the first player could drag a pearl two squares before the second player had placed anything.
  2. Two pearls heading for the same square both stay. Otherwise the order they moved in would decide games.
  3. A pearl that lands on an anchor knocks it back into its owner’s supply. So a pearl can be a weapon.
  4. The tide. After turn 40 the second row from each edge counts as shore too; after turn 50, the third row. If six drifting turns pass with no pearl moving, the tide rises a level early. A locked board does not have to wait.

There is one more: a tie in pearls goes to Dark, who moved second. Light’s first move is worth something, and the simulator measured how much. Giving ties to Dark is the smallest correction that evens it out, the way komi does in Go.

What the rules do not say

They do not say where to put your anchors. After a few games you start to see lanes: a column with a pearl in it and nothing between the pearl and your shore. You start to count pulls on your fingers before you place. Then you stop counting, because the arrows on the board show you where every pearl will drift before you confirm. That is the first thing I would tell a new player: look at the arrows, then place.

entry.title: How the computer plays
entry.summary: Four levels, one search, and why Medium looks as deep as Hard but settles for less.
entry.content:
The computer opponent in Swan Road is a plain alpha-beta search: look ahead a fixed number of turns, score the positions at the end, and pick the move that leads to the best one if the other side also plays well. No neural network. The interesting choices were how deep to look and what to do with the answer.

Three copies of the rules

The rules exist three times. A Python version was the first, written to try variants quickly. A Rust version came next, fast enough to play a hundred games against itself in a minute, and it is the one the balance work ran on. The Swift version is the one in the app.

Three versions can disagree, and a disagreement would mean the app plays a different game from the one the balance work tested. So two checks run whenever the rules change: every Python game is replayed in Rust step by step, and the Swift search is compared with the Rust search on random positions until the values match exactly. Both must stay at zero mismatches.

Added 17 November. There is now a fourth copy. Today’s puzzle plays in a browser, so the rules were written once more, in JavaScript, and held to the same standard: every legal move from every position on every solution in the puzzle book is played through the JavaScript rules and through the Python ones, and the boards must match. The puzzle in your browser has the rest.

How deep

Depth is the lever. On an iPhone 16 Plus, looking six turns ahead on the 7×7 board takes between a quarter of a second and six tenths of a second per move. One turn deeper takes three to fifteen seconds. So Expert looks six ahead and stops there, and five ahead on the bigger 9×9 board, where each turn has more moves.

  • Easy looks two ahead.
  • Medium and Hard look four ahead.
  • Expert looks six ahead.

Why Medium is not just a shallower Hard

The first Medium looked two turns ahead and picked its best move. It was no stronger than Easy. Looking three ahead was closer to Hard than to Easy. There was no depth between them that felt like a middle.

What worked was depth with a loose hand. Medium looks as far ahead as Hard, then picks at random from its three best moves, as long as they are within a band of the best. The band is sixty points, which is about six rows of pearl drift and well short of a whole pearl. It makes Medium a player who sees what Hard sees and sometimes takes the second-best road. Easy does the same with its six best moves. Hard and Expert always take the best.

The daily game

The daily game is the same board for everyone, with one try. For that to be fair, the computer has to make the same reply on every phone, and a time limit would not do it: a new phone searches more in a second than an old one. So the daily opponent stops at a fixed number of positions examined instead of a fixed time. On an iPhone 12, the longest reply stays under about eight seconds.

How strong

The campaign climbs from a gentle first opponent to Expert, and the climb was measured, not guessed: each level played hundreds of games against the others, and the rating anchors in the app come from the gaps those games showed. A strong player beats Expert about one time in twenty. For a while the daily game cycled Expert in every third day, and those days ended most streaks, so the daily now alternates Medium and Hard. Expert is still there under Play, for the days you want to lose with dignity.

entry.title: Playing without looking
entry.summary: What VoiceOver says about a square, and the other settings the game listens to.
entry.content:
A board game on a phone is mostly a picture, and a picture is the hardest thing to make work for someone who cannot see it. Swan Road was built to be played with VoiceOver from the first version, and this post is about what that took.

What a square says

Every square on the board is its own element. Touch one and VoiceOver reads a sentence built from what is there:

Row 3, column 4, pearl, drifting up, Light’s shore, pulled 3 up, 1 left.

The parts come in a fixed order so a regular player learns to listen for the one they need. The position first. Then what is on the square: a pearl, a Light anchor, a Dark anchor, or empty. For a pearl, what it will do when the turn ends: drifting up, or held when the pulls cancel or another pearl blocks the way. If a shore runs through that row, whose shore it is. Last, the pulls on the pearl, by strength and direction.

While you have a move pending but not yet confirmed, the pearls that would change say so: this move drifts it left. That is the spoken version of the arrows sighted players see before they confirm.

The tide bar has a spoken label too: Tide, or Tide up: shores 3 deep once it has risen.

Type

The text scales with the Dynamic Type setting, including the board’s captions and the rules, up into the accessibility sizes. It stops growing at the size where the board would no longer fit on the screen, so the board keeps its squares. The splash screen caps its own type at the largest standard size, since it is decorative and a tap skips it.

Motion

With Reduce Motion on, the pulsing highlight on a suggested square becomes a steady one, the puzzle animations hold still, and the opening screen shortens its fades and skips the small drop of the pearl. Nothing you need is conveyed by motion alone; the arrows and the spoken labels carry the same information.

Contrast and colour

With Increase Contrast on, secondary text brightens; in the Night look, from sixty percent of the ink colour to eighty-five. In every look, the colours were chosen so that secondary text clears a 4.5 to 1 contrast against its background.

Colour never carries meaning on its own. The two shores are told apart by position, by the names in the spoken labels, and in the Nautical chart look by hatching: Light’s shore is hatched one way and Dark’s is cross-hatched.

What it cost

Less than you would think, because most of it is the same work as making the game explain itself to anyone. The spoken label for a square is the drift preview in words. The tide bar’s label is the tide bar in words. Once the game can say what it is doing, saying it to VoiceOver is one more line.

On the website

Added 17 November. Today’s puzzle now plays in a browser, and the page follows the same idea. Each square is a button with a spoken label, a line of text reports every move and where the pearls drifted, and the arrow keys move from square to square. It has not yet had the testing the app has had. If you use a screen reader and try it, the support page is the place to say what works and what does not.
